newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-MORDT EXIT REFLECTS SPRINGBOK TURMOIL.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-MORDT EXIT REFLECTS SPRINGBOK TURMOIL.

text.p: Old wounds have been re-opened ahead of the first test between South Africa and the British Lions in Cape Town on Saturday following the resignation of former Springbok wing and selector Ray Mordt as coach of the Gauteng Lions (formerly Transvaal).

Mordt quit on Tuesday accusing members of the Springbok side who triumphed in front of president Nelson Mandela in the 1995 Rugby World Cup of being at the root of problems which have dogged South African rugby at both test and provincial level.
"I am no longer prepared to deal with certain World Cup Springboks," said Mordt. "They have created a negative environment which makes it impossible for me to continue coaching."

Mordt is not alone in claiming the current climate of unrest should be laid at the door of the members of the Springbok squad which won the World Cup almost exactly two years ago. His erstwhile boss, Louis Luyt, has been saying it ever since he brokered the multi-million dollar deal which has sparked much of the ill-feeling.

Luyt, president of both the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) and the Transvaal Rugby Union (TRU), has accused the players of "bleeding the game", yet it was Luyt himself who effectively handed the players their power with his reaction to Ross Turnbull's proposed breakaway World Rugby Corporation (WRC), backed by Australian media magnate Kerry Packer.

In his book "One Team, One Country", Edward Griffiths, the chief executive of SARFU during the World Cup year, reveals how Luyt called the Transvaal Springboks to his home in Johannesburg on June 30, 1995 to make a rival offer.

Griffiths wrote: "The SARFU president looked (Francois) Pienaar directly in the eye and said the four words which would solve the problem at the time, but create enormous difficulties for South African rugby later: "I will match Packer", Luyt said."

For all Luyt's business acumen, the deal gave massive sums to the players and put into perspective the 10-year, 500 million US dollar deal between Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation and the newly-created body SANZAR (South Africa, New Zealand, Australia Rugby).
SARFU's share of the money from Murdoch's contract is 20 million US dollars a year, but the 27 World Cup Springboks accounted for almost a quarter of that amount.

When the dust settled, Luyt began to look at ways of cutting costs. He did not stand in the way of the decision to oust Pienaar from the national squad and when the popular captain together with Rudolf Straeuli and Joel Stransky opted to play in England, Luyt welcomed the moves as a way to get them off the SARFU payroll.

Now, after a disappointing end to Gauteng's Super 12 season, Mordt has also pointed the finger at the World Cup Springboks, saying: "I really don't believe the problem will be resolved until August next year when the contracts of certain players expire".

As for the players, their lucrative World Cup contracts do not allow them to voice their own side of the story. The contracts contain a confidentiality clause which forbids the players from talking to the media.

Lock Kobus Wiese, who took over the Gauteng captaincy from Pienaar, said: "I can't say anything now, I've been told not to. But in time we can tell our side of the story. It's easy to blame players when things go wrong".

Hennie Le Roux, who has played only once for Gauteng since Luyt accused him of feigning injury against Auckland and sent him home, said: "There are obviously problems, deeper maybe than any public perceptions, but it is not right to air these now and point fingers. That won't help anybody".

There has been a lot of finger pointing since that day in June 1995 when the Springboks seemed to have united the country when Mandela, clad in an identical number 6 jersey, presented the World Cup to Pienaar .

Last year Henry Tromp, once jailed for manslaughter, was selected to play for the national side. The old South African flag was waved at test matches. Finance minister Trevor Manuel cheered for the All Blacks against the all-white Springboks. This year began with the resignation of Springbok coach Andre Markgraaff who was heard on a clandestinely made tape to use the hated word "kaffir".

The development programme was accused of tokenism, despite the amount of money spent on it. Coloured businessman Brian van Rooyen has made allegations of financial irregularities over sponsorship and TV deals and presented a 500-page document to a government task force, who have yet to report back. Van Rooyen and other disaffected administrators from the pre-unification rugby boards then tried to have the Lions tour banned at the last minute.
The one thing that seemed to be in place, a Springbok team good enough to beat the Lions, also now seems in danger from the ripples caused by Mordt's resignation.

Before the tour began the Lions were written off as no-hopers, but their performances in the last three tour games, with wins over Gauteng, Natal and the Emerging Springboks, has transformed their prospects for the first test.
Add into the equation a union at war with itself and a series win for the Lions suddenly appears more than just a pipe-dream.
